grammar.title: Future in the Past (was about to, was to, would)
grammar.explanation:
Sometimes we talk about the past and describe what was in the future at that time. For this we use **would**, **was about to**, **was on the point of**, **was to**, and **was to have done**.

**Would** is the past form of will. We use it after past reporting verbs, for example when an articulate speaker said she **would** present her academic journal article the next day.

**Was about to** means something was very near in the future at that time. It is often interrupted, as in: she **was about to** leave when the phone rang.

**Was on the point of** is even nearer than was about to. It takes an -ing form, so we say she **was on the point of** giving up, not to give up.

**Was to** describes destiny or an official plan seen from the past. In stories it tells us what really happened later, as in: they met in 1990, and they **were to** marry ten years later.

**Was to have done** describes a plan that did not happen. The meeting **was to have taken** place at ten, but it was cancelled, and the annual bonus **was to have been** paid in December, but it was delayed.
examples: *I knew he **would** never see her again.* (would — future seen from the past)
*We **were about to** have dinner when the guests arrived.* (about to — very near future, interrupted)
*He **was on the point of** resigning when they offered him a promotion.* (on the point of — just about to)
*She **was to** become one of the most famous writers of her time.* (was to — destiny)
*The new hospital **was to have been** opened in 2020, but the work was delayed.* (was to have been — a plan that failed)

practice.q: Rewrite using would: She said, "I will call you tomorrow."
practice.a: She said she would call me the next day.

practice.q: Rewrite using was about to: I almost left when the phone rang.
practice.a: I was about to leave when the phone rang.

practice.q: Rewrite using was on the point of: She almost gave up, and then she found the answer in an academic journal.
practice.a: She was on the point of giving up when she found the answer in an academic journal.

practice.q: Rewrite using was to have done: The new shelter was planned to open in spring, but the work was delayed.
practice.a: The new shelter was to have been opened in spring, but the work was delayed.
